title: Americans Suddenly Love Japan, Not Because It's Cheap, But Because It's Normal
dek: The real driver of Japan's tourism boom isn't the exchange rate, it's the functionality of public space—clean subways, on time, no trash. What American visitors experience in Tokyo is a society where entropy has been paused.
why: This episode uses expert interviews and a listener survey to break down "why everyone's going to Japan" into six verifiable reasons. The second half, contrasting Japanese craft culture with American dysfunction, is especially worth hearing.
who: People curious about the Japan tourism phenomenon, founders and investors judging consumer and cultural trends, and readers who want to understand the contrast with American social dysfunction.

points.body: The questioner, Lisa, is a Japanese person living in Tokyo. She made a visitor calendar from November 2022 to April 2026, with green cells marking when someone visited. She counted 119 people, 96 of them her own guests, averaging one person every five days, or 20% of all her days. She says she spends all her free time helping visiting friends plan itineraries. This data visualization is itself evidence of a problem out of control, and the starting point for the question this episode answers.

points.h: Japan is poor in resources, rich in story
points.body: Roland Kelts argues the first reason for American interest in Japan isn't economic, it's story. He says Japan has almost no natural resources, no oil, very little land, only small rice paddies, but a story culture that's astonishing. The world's first novel is Japan's The Tale of Genji, a thousand years old. Through manga, anime, and the internet, the world discovered this narrative capacity. This didn't start in the 90s—Roland says there were two earlier waves: Japanism in late 19th-century Europe, and the Beat and hippie fascination with Zen and Buddhist concepts in the 50s and 60s.

David Marks points out that for seventy years after WWII, mainstream America felt fear, not affection, toward Japan. Before 1945 Japan was an enemy nation, then seen as a developing country rebuilding. In the 70s and 80s it became anxiety about Japanese economic power, with Michael Crichton's Rising Sun casting Japan as the villain. After the Cold War, there was even a CIA position paper discussing whether Japan should be the next enemy. When Japan's bubble burst in the 90s, America felt a sense of relief. When David moved to Japan in 2003, having a friend visit was the event of the year, because nobody came.

points.h: The government made Japan cheap by hand
points.body: The third wave was a government plan. In 2003, Junichiro Koizumi launched the Visit Japan campaign, aiming to raise tourists from 5 million to 10 million a year, with ads full of Western stereotypes of geisha, cherry blossoms, and temples. But what really worked was Shinzo Abe deliberately weakening the yen in the 2010s, originally to help exports, which made hotels and restaurants cheap for foreigners. Roland says you can eat a very good soba lunch in Tokyo for under $10, while in New York $10 won't even buy an apple and a banana. In 2013 Abe relaxed visas for Thailand and Malaysia, then China and Indonesia; Asian tourists surged first, followed by Europe and America.

points.h: Japan's functionality is the biggest draw
points.body: Roland says the most important reason is functionality. Public spaces in many countries, especially the US, have become dysfunctional: parks dirty and dangerous, rail systems terrible, airports a mess. In Japan, things just work. PJ adds that American ears hear complaints about poor public order and dirty subways as elitist, rich people's complaints. But in Japan, wanting a clean subway isn't elitism—it's the opposite: why shouldn't public things be good? On Tokyo streets you see no trash, not even cigarette butts, and smell no urine or feces. PJ says this isn't the reason for a first visit, but it might be the reason some people go again.

The sixth reason is craft. The Japanese word shokunin means artisan, someone who makes things extremely well, and such people are still respected in Japan, a tradition dating back to the 17th-century Edo period, when makers ranked above merchants. Roland tells of an animation industry person explaining the Walmart model to him: in America, the company selling the goods comes first, nobody cares who made it, a $5 pillow is made by someone who knows nothing about pillows. But in Japan, the person who makes a pillow extremely well is most valued. He took an American friend to a ramen shop, where they bought a ticket and were told to come back at 3pm; after eating, the friend said it was the best soup of his life, then asked why they don't franchise. Roland said because franchising would mean losing control over the noodles, scallions, pork bone broth, and bamboo shoots—their scallions come from a man named Sato in Chiba who's been doing it for years.

points.h: Listener survey and experts almost perfectly overlap
points.body: Search Engine sent a questionnaire to hundreds of thousands of listeners and got a flood of responses. Nearly half mentioned culture; some said they binge-watched anime as kids, played Nintendo and Sony, were fans of Pokemon and One Piece. About a quarter mentioned the weak yen; one said the exchange rate was the best in 30 years. Others mentioned craft. What pleased PJ most were the reasons only a big survey could capture: someone decided to go because of FOMO after seeing so many others go, someone went to see the Godzilla museum—Godzilla brought in five listeners. And one-on-one stories: someone went to Japan to see the work of legendary bonsai master Mazuhiko Kimura; someone fell in love at 18, lost touch over a decade later, and the only way to meet again was to fly to Japan, where they ended up spending four magical days in Osaka.

points.h: Japan is a place where entropy is paused
points.body: Listeners' enthusiasm for functionality exceeded PJ's expectations. One said they took their family to Japan to show them what a high-functioning society actually looks like, everything on time, perfectly clean. One said public toilets are everywhere, with bidets, because everyone has to poop, and poop on your butt is disgusting. One said if every country respected each other like the Japanese do with their punctuality and queuing, the world would be much better. PJ himself says he still loves America, loves that anarchic mix, but feels something broke ten years ago—not just politics, drivers are angrier, people are angrier, elbows are sharper, more people watching TikTok without headphones on the subway. He says America is like a quirky friend who turned from quirky to not-so-good quirky, which helps explain Japan's appeal.

quotes.text: My question was, why is every single person I know going to Japan or talking about going to Japan?

I often say that Japan is very poor in natural resources. There's no oil here, very little land. You know, you can grow rice, but only in these tiny rice paddies. It's a small country, but it's very rich in stories.

A lot of countries around the world, particularly the U.S., have become dysfunctional. And I say that in terms of public space. The parks are dirty and dangerous. The railway system is atrocious. The airports are a mess. And when you're in Japan, things just work.
In America, one way you can show you care about society is to ride the dirty subway. In Japan, one way you can show you care about society is to be really invested in the subway being clean.

He said, so if you go into Walmart, you can buy a $5 pillow. And it was made by people who know nothing about pillows. They don't care about pillows. They're working in some factory in Southeast Asia or China. And he said, that's the Walmart model. But he said, in Japan, we actually think the person who made the pillow and made it really well is the most valuable person.
I took my family to Japan so they could see what a high-functioning society really looks like, where everything runs on time, is perfectly clean.
